summary: Neural architecture: frozen Qwen3-4B with float32 LoRA adapters and a zero-initialised cross-attention latent bridge; experience tokenizer with a separate exact-value channel; causal experiential core with gated persistent slots and a direct current-event path; decision trunk and unit-norm feature map; Bayesian fast state (exact Gaussian / NIG, Laplace GLM with censoring, forgetting, change detection) with a learned prior; CamLiveModel implementing nn.api.LatentModelAPI; measured presets 5M-1B; benchmark and fast-adaptation comparison with recorded evidence.

NA-01.limitations: Qwen/Qwen3-4B (4,022,468,096 parameters, bf16, frozen, pinned revision) is the only backbone loaded and tested; Qwen3-8B is a configuration change that was not run. Texts longer than max_text_tokens are cut to head 3/4 + tail 1/4 (counted in backbone.stats), not chunked. Single-stream generation speed is bounded by per-step Python overhead on this shared machine (on par with transformers' own generate, measured).

NA-02.limitations: Measured 50,953,765 experiential parameters (d_model 768, 6 blocks, 12 heads, d_ff 1024, 8 slots, 128 features); config.SCALE_PRESETS itself still holds d_ff=1792 (would give 67.8 M) - corrected inside nn/presets.py, change request A-1. The semantic projection of this preset is low-rank (7680 -> 384 -> 768).

NA-03.limitations: 16,713,856 adapter parameters = LoRA rank 32 on q_proj/v_proj of all 36 layers (11,796,480) + latent bridge (4,917,376). k_proj / o_proj / MLP projections carry no adapter in the default configuration.

NA-04.limitations: Reward and other-head counts are zero in the evidence file because those modules are registered by Workstreams B/C/D (register_head); count_parameters reports them per head once registered (tested with stand-in heads).

NA-05.limitations: Verified at initialisation and on small synthetic learning problems (8-step recall); whether the representations become useful abstractions is a question for training on real experience (Workstreams D / S). phi is bounded (unit norm) but NOT well-conditioned on realistic inputs at initialisation: real configuration, 2304 realistic combinations: Gram max/min eigenvalue 2.3e4, 90 % of the mass in 23 of 128 directions; one query alone 4.5e5 (participation ratio 2.0). The float64 fast layer stays exact on such features (tested). Candidates that differ in one argument: cos(z) 0.747 on Qwen3-4B (was 0.9997); one of several argument leaves changing moves z less (bag of leaves).

NA-07.limitations: One posterior per outcome kind (real, count, binary, time-to-event); categorical outcomes are not modelled by the fast layer (change request A-5). Non-Gaussian updates are Laplace approximations: the mode is exact (monotone safeguarded search to |step| <= 1e-11 (1 + |eta|), cap 100 iterations, measured <= 7 iterations for counts / time-to-event and <= 16 for 1e9 binomial trials; iterations and convergence are returned). [DX, G2L-1] The count / time-to-event search takes the convex G-step from the left of the root too, and 'converged' is reported only where the root condition holds at the returned point (relative residual <= 1e-8 plus the float64 rounding of the prior term, or the log-form residual <= 1e-8): before, 4 of 2625 extreme count problems (prior predictor >= 16 orders below the count, e.g. eta0 -30, count 1e9 at exposure 1e-12) reported convergence at eta 3.3e11 / 1e15 instead of 48.35; now all 2625 equal a float64 bisection to <= 1e-9 (tests/nn/test_dx_fast_mode.py; G2-learn probe_fast_stress.py 46/46). The Laplace shape is Gaussian. Time-to-event uses a constant-hazard (exponential) likelihood. The learned dispersion exp(disp_raw) (1 at init) tempers count likelihoods only. Inferred-noise Gaussian: predict() returns the Student-t predictive variance (b/(a-1))(1+q); posterior()['cov'] / ['noise'] are the scale (b/a)V and b/a. Impossible observations raise ValueError (stateful update and online_nll).

NA-09.limitations: Shown on Qwen3-4B: all 72 LoRA modules and every bridge tensor receive gradient through the embedding path and through generation_logprob, and with the backbone loaded in float32 central finite differences along the analytic gradient equal its norm to 3 % for every path (embedding -> LoRA-B, generation -> LoRA-B, -> zero-init bridge, -> latent, -> all adapters, -> bridge -> b -> experiential weights). generation_logprob / the sampler use a float32 output layer (head error on the same hidden states 0.0000 nats, was up to 0.143); the bf16 decoder trunk still differs from the float32 model by up to 0.36 nats on a one-token completion, and the KV-cache sampler differs from generation_logprob by up to 0.073 nats per token. Caches follow the adapter content (also .data writes). NOT shown here: adapter updates driven by real experience (Workstream D's schedule).

NA-10.limitations: All presets are instantiated and counted on CPU; only the 50m preset was run on GPU (forward/backward step measured). The 150m-1b presets were never trained or benchmarked, and no learning-speed comparison across scales was made here.

NA-11.limitations: A token carries at most max_values (4) quantities; to_items continues longer lists in further items, while the candidate-action encoder keeps the first 4 cost quantities (dropped ones are counted in tokenizer.stats). Action targets / arguments: up to 16 leaves through the value channel (numbers exact + hashed identity of every leaf), further leaves dropped and counted (stats['dropped_arguments']). Metric names are hashed into 2 x 2048 buckets (collisions possible). Relations and entities are text items; there is no graph structure.

NA-12.limitations: The bridge is cross-attention from the decoder's residual stream to bridge_tokens virtual prefix tokens, not tokens placed in the sequence (a literal zero prefix is not a no-op: measured logit change up to 1.0469; change request A-2). Shown: exact no-op at init, non-zero gradient, and that one optimisation step makes next-token probabilities depend on the latent. NOT shown: that a trained bridge improves the quality of generated candidate actions (needs training on experience; Workstreams B / D).

NA-13.limitations: See scientific_failures for where the learned prior loses (small support on Gaussian targets; fixed-noise variant; point accuracy on held-out Gaussian families; in-distribution ranking against a larger GRU; only a marginal lead on held-out counts). Synthetic meta-regression only (2-d inputs, 4 training and 3 held-out function families, 2 seeds, 600 evaluation tasks per split); it says nothing yet about real experience. The significance figures pool tasks that share one trained model per seed. Re-run with the converged GLM updates and the count-only dispersion (exp(disp_raw), 1 at init): Gaussian numbers unchanged to 4 decimals; count numbers changed (the BLR baseline, a Laplace GLM, improved most). Verdicts: {"gaussian": "held-out families: winner = learned_prior_bayes; ranking = ['learned_prior_bayes', 'blr_raw', 'gru', 'running_stats']; learned prior WINS", "count": "held-out families: winner = learned_prior_bayes; ranking = ['learned_prior_bayes', 'gru', 'blr_raw', 'running_stats']; learned prior WINS"}

measured.speed_note: params.json was measured at CPU load average ~26 on a GPU shared with another tenant: speeds are lower bounds (the earlier recording ran at load ~5: 24.1 / 192.7 generation tokens/s). The cost of the fixes was measured in the same process instead: float32 output layer ~4 % of generation speed; batch-invariant embedding forwards 67-79 % of dynamic-padding throughput for large uncached calls, 40-70 % for one to four short texts; cached call of 64 texts 1.5 ms.

embedding_batch_invariance_ab_tokens_per.note: same process, best of 3, loaded machine (before the extra padding column, +1 position per row)

generation_tokens_per_s_same_process_ab.note: same process, interleaved, best of 3 x 96 greedy tokens; the float32 output layer costs about 4 %

float32_output_layer.source: docs/verification/repro/nn/probe_real_backbone.py --part gradsave / fd32 / misc (rerun on the final code)

not_done: Qwen3-8B (or any other backbone than Qwen/Qwen3-4B) was not loaded or tested; it is a configuration change only.

Presets 150m, 500m and 1b are instantiated and counted on CPU only: never trained, never run on GPU. No experiment here shows whether more experiential capacity helps (spec 16.10 asks for that comparison; it needs the learner and evaluation of Workstreams D / S).
config.SCALE_PRESETS (master-owned) still holds the overshooting d_ff values; the corrected numbers live in nn/presets.py (change request A-1).
The latent bridge is cross-attention to virtual prefix tokens, not prefix tokens inside the sequence (change request A-2). Its usefulness after training on experience is not evaluated here.

Adapter learning from real experience is not demonstrated here: only that both gradient paths work on the real backbone and that an optimizer step changes behaviour. The slow adapter schedule is Workstream D's.
The fast layer does not model categorical outcomes; time-to-event is constant-hazard only; one posterior per outcome kind (not per metric).
The fast-adaptation comparison is synthetic (no real experience data).
tokenize(with_grad=True) over whole contexts is memory-heavy; grad_last=k is provided but encode_decisions (master-owned) does not pass it yet (change request A-3).
The backbone wrapper keeps the active bridge memory and capture buffers as instance state: one model must not run generation / embedding from several threads at once.
Long texts are truncated (head 3/4 + tail 1/4 of max_text_tokens), not chunked; truncation is counted in backbone.stats['truncated_tokens'].

No merged-LoRA inference path: with non-zero adapters generation is 8-9 % slower than the bare backbone (measured by the verifier's probe on the final code); the float32 output layer costs another ~4 % (same-process A/B: 22.1 vs 23.0 tokens/s at batch 1, 177.4 vs 184.3 at batch 8). The tiny test backbone has no KV cache.
The bf16 trunk is not made more precise: generation_logprob vs the float32 model up to 0.36 nats on a one-token completion (see scientific_failures).
tests/nn/test_fast_compare.py still checks only the structure of the recorded comparison (a full re-run takes ~1 h); the recorded numbers were regenerated with the final code.
scientific_failures: Gaussian targets, small support: the learned-prior Bayesian layer is WORSE than the recurrent baseline before it has seen about three points - held-out families NLL at k=0: 1.6995 vs GRU 1.4188 vs running statistics 1.467 (a unit normal scores 1.4189); at k=1: 1.5156 vs GRU 1.3854; in-distribution k=0: 1.6896 vs GRU 1.3495. It wins from k=3 on (k=3: 1.3269 vs 1.3325; k=8: 1.0869 vs 1.1449; k=31: 0.6137 vs 1.0467). Cause: the conjugate normal-inverse-gamma prior ties the weight uncertainty to the uncertain noise scale, which makes the prior predictive heavy-tailed. (docs/evidence/A/fast_adaptation.json)

Gaussian targets, fixed learned noise instead of inferred noise: FAILS on held-out families - mean NLL 1.9933 (per seed [1.9935, 1.9931]) vs 0.8909 with inferred noise, and worse than running statistics (1.4483); it becomes over-confident as evidence accumulates (k=31: 2.1035). In-distribution it is calibrated at k=0 (1.3458) but still behind overall (0.2988 vs 0.2132). The inferred-noise mode is therefore the default. (docs/evidence/A/fast_adaptation_noise_mode.json)

Count targets, held-out families: the learned-prior layer is only marginally ahead of / level with the GRU with a negative-binomial head - mean NLL 2.6237 vs 2.6381 (difference -0.0144 +- 0.008, z = -1.8, tasks pooled over 2 seeds). Not a robust win. (docs/evidence/A/fast_adaptation.json, re-run with the converged GLM updates)

Gaussian targets, held-out families, point accuracy: the GRU has the lower RMSE of the predictive mean (0.8185 vs 0.8629 for the learned prior, mean over support sizes >= 1); the learned prior wins on calibrated uncertainty (NLL), not on point accuracy.

Gaussian targets, training families: the recorded lead (learned prior 0.2132 vs GRU 0.5753) reflects the size of the recorded GRU (hidden 64, 8000 steps), not an advantage of the Bayesian layer: the verifier's run with a GRU of hidden 256 trained 16000 steps reached 0.1825 vs 0.2206 on seed 0 (docs/verification/G_nn.md section 4; not re-run here). On held-out families the wider GRUs transfer worse (1.38 / 1.93 vs 0.89).

Ill-conditioned features at initialisation (not fixed): on realistic inputs of the real configuration the phi Gram has max/min eigenvalue 2.3e4 over all queries (4.5e5 for one query, participation ratio 2.0); only the numerical exactness of the fast layer on such features is shown.

generation_logprob is not accurate to 0.05 nats per token against the same model in float32: with the float32 output layer the bf16 decoder trunk still gives -0.16 / -0.36 / +0.12 / -0.05 / -0.00 nats for completions of 1 / 1 / 11 / 1 / 2 tokens (the head was not the main error); the KV-cache sampler and generation_logprob differ by up to 0.073 nats per token.
